title: Interfaces and abstract classes
summary: Contracts, partial implementations, and programming to an interface.

recallPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
What does "program to an interface, not an implementation" mean?
How do interfaces make code easier to test?

mentalModel.analogy: An interface is a **job description**: it lists what the role must do, and anyone who can do those things can be hired. An abstract class is a **half-built house** from a developer: the foundations and walls are done and shared, and each buyer finishes the rooms their own way.

sections.heading: Interfaces: a contract
sections.body:
An **interface** declares **what** a type can do, as method signatures, without saying **how**. Any class that implements all of them can be used wherever the interface is expected.

- A class can implement **many** interfaces (`Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Clickable`…), even in languages with single class inheritance.
- Interfaces normally hold no instance state. Java and Kotlin interfaces can have **default methods** with shared behaviour; Kotlin's can also declare properties.
- TypeScript interfaces are **structural**: any object with the right shape fits, even without `implements`. Python uses `ABC` with `@abstractmethod`, or `typing.Protocol` for structural typing (duck typing that type checkers can verify).

sections.heading: Abstract classes: a partial implementation
sections.body:
An **abstract class** can't be instantiated. It can hold **state**, **constructors** and **finished methods**, alongside **abstract methods** that subclasses must fill in.

It suits a family of closely related classes that share real code. A `Shape` base might store a name and implement `describe()` using an abstract `area()` that each shape supplies. That is the **template method** pattern.

| Feature | Interface | Abstract class |
|---|---|---|
| Instance state | No (only constants or properties) | Yes |
| Constructors | No | Yes |
| Implemented methods | Default methods only | Any |
| How many per class | Many | One (Java, Kotlin, TS) |
| Relationship | can-do (capability) | is-a (family) |

sections.heading: Which one to use
sections.body:
- Use an **interface** to describe a **capability** that unrelated classes might share (`Comparable`, `Closeable`, `PaymentProcessor`), or whenever you just want a contract. This is the default choice.
- Use an **abstract class** when closely related classes share **state and real code**, and you want a common base with a few gaps to fill.
- You can combine them: an interface for the contract, plus an abstract base that implements the boring parts.

In interviews, mention that interfaces avoid the single-inheritance limit, and that abstract classes are where shared state lives.

sections.heading: Program to an interface
sections.body:
**Program to an interface, not an implementation** means variables, parameters and fields should be typed by what you need (`List`, `PaymentProcessor`), not by a specific class (`ArrayList`, `StripeProcessor`).

Then any implementation can be passed in:

- **Swapping** is cheap: change the payment provider in one place.
- **Testing** is easy: pass a **fake** that records calls, or a **mock** from a library, instead of hitting a real payment API.
- **Parallel work**: one team builds against the interface while another implements it.

This is the same idea as dependency inversion from SOLID, seen from the caller's side.

explainBack.prompt: Explain the difference between an interface and an abstract class, when you would use each, and how programming to an interface helps with testing.

rubric.point: An interface is a contract: what a type can do, not how.
A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class (in Java, Kotlin, TS).
An abstract class can hold state, constructors and finished methods, plus abstract gaps for subclasses.
Interface for a capability or contract; abstract class for related classes sharing real code.
Type variables and parameters by the interface, so any implementation can be passed in.
Tests can then pass a fake or mock instead of the real dependency.

checks.prompt: Which of these can you create an instance of directly with `new` (or by calling it in Python)?
checks.explanation: Only concrete classes can be instantiated. Interfaces and abstract classes have gaps that something else must fill.

hints.text: Which one has no missing pieces?

checks.prompt: Several related classes need the same fields and some identical methods, but each computes one value differently. What fits best?
options: An abstract base class with one abstract method
Copy the code into each class
checks.explanation: Shared state and shared methods belong in an abstract class. The one varying calculation is the abstract method each subclass supplies.

hints.text: Which one can hold fields and finished methods?

checks.prompt: Unrelated classes (`Invoice`, `Photo`, `Song`) all need to be exportable. What fits best?
options: Make them all extend a common Exportable base class
Put export logic in a global if/else
Make them all subclasses of Photo
checks.explanation: A capability shared by unrelated classes is an interface. A shared base class would force an odd is-a relationship and use up their one superclass.

hints.text: Is an invoice the same kind of thing as a song?

checks.prompt: In Java or Kotlin, a class can…
options: extend many classes and implement one interface
extend one class and implement many interfaces
extend one class and implement one interface
checks.explanation: Single class inheritance, multiple interface implementation. That is why capabilities are usually interfaces.

hints.text: Which one avoids the diamond problem?

checks.prompt: Why declare a parameter as `PaymentProcessor` rather than `StripeProcessor`?
options: It makes the code run faster.
Any implementation can then be passed in, including a fake in tests, and the provider can change without touching this code.
checks.explanation: Programming to an interface decouples the caller from one implementation. That is what makes swapping and testing cheap.

hints.text: What would a unit test pass in?

checks.prompt: In TypeScript, an object literal with the right methods is accepted where an interface is expected, even without `implements`. Why?
options: TypeScript's type system is structural: it checks the shape, not the declared name
checks.explanation: TypeScript compares shapes (structural typing). Java and Kotlin are nominal: a class must say it implements the interface.

hints.text: Does TypeScript care what a type is called, or what it contains?

checks.prompt: In Python, how do you make a method that every subclass must implement?
options: Name it with a leading underscore
Inherit from abc.ABC and decorate the method with @abstractmethod
checks.explanation: A class with an unimplemented `@abstractmethod` can't be instantiated. `typing.Protocol` is the structural alternative, checked by type checkers.

hints.text: There is a standard library module for abstract base classes.

checks.prompt: Kotlin and Java interfaces can include method bodies. What are those called, and what can't the interface still hold?
options: Default methods; interfaces still can't hold instance state set through a constructor
Static classes; they can't hold methods
Abstract methods; they can't hold constants
checks.explanation: Default methods share behaviour across implementations. Per-instance state and constructors remain the job of classes.

hints.text: They provide a default behaviour that implementations may override.

checks.prompt: An abstract `Shape.describe()` calls the abstract `area()`, which each subclass supplies. What is this design called?
checks.explanation: The base class fixes the overall algorithm and leaves specific steps to subclasses: the template method pattern.

hints.text: The base class provides a template with blanks.

checks.prompt: In a test, you pass a `FakePaymentProcessor` that records amounts instead of charging cards. What does that rely on?
options: Checkout depending on a PaymentProcessor interface
checks.explanation: Because Checkout depends on the interface, any implementation fits, including a fake that just records calls.

hints.text: What type is Checkout's processor field?

handsOn.prompt:
Write a checkout that works with **any** payment processor.

- A `PaymentProcessor` interface with `pay(amount)`, returning a receipt string.
- `Checkout(processor)` with `add(price)` and `pay()`. `pay()` charges the total through the processor and returns its receipt. Paying an empty basket throws an error.
- A `FakeProcessor` for tests: it records every amount in a `charged` list and returns `"paid X"`, with X to 2 decimal places, e.g. `"paid 5.00"`.

How does this let you test `Checkout` without a real payment provider?

hints.text: Checkout should only know about the interface, never a concrete processor.
Program to an interface, and inject the implementation.

Checkout stores the processor and a list of prices. pay() sums them, throws if empty, otherwise returns processor.pay(total). FakeProcessor pushes the amount onto charged and returns the receipt string.

handsOn.explanation: `Checkout` depends only on the `PaymentProcessor` contract, so a test passes a `FakeProcessor` and asserts on `charged` and the receipt: no network, no real money, fast and repeatable. Production passes a real processor. Switching providers is a new class plus one line where it is injected, and `Checkout` itself never changes.
selfCheck: Checkout's field and constructor are typed by the interface, not a concrete class.
The fake records amounts, so a test can assert what was charged.
I explained how the fake avoids calling a real provider.

commonMistakes.mistake: Saying interfaces and abstract classes are interchangeable.
commonMistakes.fix: Interfaces are contracts a class can have many of; abstract classes share state and code but use up the single superclass.

commonMistakes.mistake: Typing parameters by the concrete class.
commonMistakes.fix: Type them by the interface, so any implementation, including a test fake, can be passed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating a shared base class for unrelated types.
commonMistakes.fix: Unrelated types sharing a capability want an interface.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking TypeScript needs `implements` for a type to fit an interface.
commonMistakes.fix: TypeScript is structural: matching the shape is enough. `implements` just checks it early.
Use `abc.ABC` with `@abstractmethod` for enforced contracts, or `typing.Protocol` for structural ones.
Depend on an interface and pass a fake or mock in tests.
